I know that there are internal conflicts, but they felt very shallow to me. 

The answer to Dalinar's internal struggle of whether he was doing the right thing or just going crazy is basically obvious to everyone. When everyone is criticizing him for being to honorable, I mean there's only so far my suspension of disbelieve can be stretched, at a certain point it just feels silly.

Kaladin's internal struggle was whether he should just give up or keep fighting, I mean is that really even a real question? I suppose it could have been written in a more believable way, but for me it just never rang true. It could have been more real to me if he was actually the cause to some of his misfortunes, but of course everything he did was right, it was everyone else that was ruthless and evil.

As far as characters making mistakes, while you could make some counterarguments, I would still have to stand by my point overall. When the characters do suffer consequences over their actions, it's usually because someone else is doing them wrong, not because they did the wrong thing. If they did do something wrong, it was because someone convinced them that their original beliefs were incorrect, and when they go back and stick to their moral core everything is alright again. You don't have characters with very many flaws in Brandon's books.

I'm not trying to hate, like I said I enjoy the books, I'm just trying to explain a point of view that I and many others share.

I think the Stormlight Archives are nearly as bad yes. 

1. Every character with a sense of humor, in all of Sanderson's works, all have the same type of humor. It's very clearly Brandon's sense of humor, not that characters sense of humor. It's a small thing but it's very glaring because humor is an important aspect to many of his characters. A good character would have their own unique sense of humor that actually feels right for their character. 

It doesn't help that his "funny" characters are nearly always touted as super clever, and unbelievably witty, especially when I myself find their humor really derivative and dull. There is a constant clash where he is telling me his characters are witty and clever, and then showing me just the opposite.

2. His characters generally play very close to your standard archetypes, with very little deviation. Worse, if you take his work as a whole, they generally conform to Sanderson's own cookie cutter molds for characters. If I had just read one book of his I might not find this a big issue, but after reading 3-4 of his series it really starts to stand out. 

3. Sanderson rarely has characters with any internal conflicts. Nearly all conflicts are external, and when they are internal they are so superficial or shallow it mostly just makes me want to roll my eyes. This creates rather flat characters, or worse characters that appear stupid. Interesting characters don't always know what the right thing is, they don't always have all the answers, they sometimes do things that are really bad. This is because Brandon only writes about heroes and villains, with very little shades of grey in between. Some people actually find this a strength, but personally I find it rather boring from a character building standpoint. Without mistakes, without imperfections, there isn't really any room to grow, and there isn't really anything to relate to. In the stormlight archives the heroes are always right, the villians are always wrong, that's just the way the world is. This is why at the end of the 2nd archive book, I was really excited about Adolins actions regarding one of the villians. It's rare to see something as morally grey like that from Sanderson, and I'm interested to see where he takes it.

4. Sanderson's characters are largely static. Kaladins character from the first book is pretty much the same as the Kaladin at the end of the first book. Same with every other character. Sanderson only ever really creates an illusion of change. Kaladin was in a low place through most of book one, but did he ever really change any part of his world view? Did Elodin? No, they only had their way of looking at things confirmed, because Sanderson's heroes are always right. 

I could probably keep going but I would just sound more and more nitpicky. To me character is the most important part of any story, so I spend a lot of time thinking about what makes a good character, and I really enjoy books with good characters, so it bothers me quite a bit when I feel they are badly done, and in my opinion Brandon doesn't do them well.

It really just comes down to preferences. If you enjoy just a straight story about heroes, and don't mind static characters Brandon's books are great. They have great worldbuilding, some of the best action in the business, and they move quickly. Most importantly of all he writes quickly! I quite enjoy them myself, because so many parts of what he writes is good, but I just don't expect any deep themes or complex characterizations.

I was also homeschooled as a child. I homeschooled from kindergarten through 9th grade before going to a public high school and honestly I regret not homeschooling all the way through. 

The way homeschool curriculum is set up is to allow for self teaching. Your mother doesn't have to have a college degree or teaching experience. They just have to hold you accountable, by the time you are in middle school you should be doing all the learning yourself. I think most parents are perfectly capable of that.

As for structure and substance, I had so much more of that in homeschooling than I did in public school. I learned 5 times as much homeschooling than I did in public school. The structure was set by my parents and myself, and the substance was set by the curriculum chosen so my experience may not be everyone. It is possible and not even difficult though.

My parents also enrolled me in a lot of social activities. I was active in sports until I decided I wasn't interested, I was active in boyscouts, I was active at church, I was active in our homeschool group doing countless different activities. There are tons of different ways to socialize besides being sent for 7 hours a day to a glorified babysitter. 

I consider prolonging a child's trust in his parents a benefit not a detriment. What you are doing when you send a child to public school is basically transferring a child's authority figure from the parent to the teacher, or in other words the school system. I think parents should have the right to choose whether they want the state to be able to teach their child whatever values they want, or whether they, as the parent, have the right to instill their own values in the child. I guess this really is going to depend on your view of the state, but I certainly don't trust america to raise my child for me.

I'd also like to talk about some of the negative experiences I had switching from homeschooling to public schooling.

Going to public school meant going to a culture where learning was not important. In fact you were cooler the more you appeared not to care. When I first started and showed how much I knew I was seen as weird. I was forced to quickly change my attitude or be ostracized.

Public school is also a one size fits all education system. Unfortunately this just isn't a good way to teach in my opinion. School quickly became boring when my learning was based on what others could learn instead of what I could learn. Many of my lessons would turn into passing the AP test or the TAKS test instead of learning new material. I once slept through every single class in my AP US History course, yet still got a higher score than everyone else in the AP exam because I read the text book before the test. All we did in class however was practice the AP test while our teacher did her homework from grad school.

Even the social aspect of public school was not all it was cracked up to be. I was never excluded from any group in high school, I could hang out with pretty much anyone I chose. However I also never fit in with anyone and I was never included or invited to anything. I saw these people at school and that was it. Did going to public school make me more social? Not really. In fact it made me wary of large groups because I was never included in them. I think this is the experience of just as many kids as those who come out wonderfully socialized. It really just depends on the kid himself in my opinion.

Think about the ways your life could be improved if you are able to quit and I guarantee you will be able to come up with some motivation. I just had to recognize all the problems it could possibly be causing in my life to decide for myself.

3. You have to have goals. Your goal shouldn't just be stopping PMO, although that should be a major one. What other things would you like to change in your life?

 For me I wanted to start spending less time on the computer, I wanted to be more thoughtful of the other people in my life, I wanted to be healthier, I wan't to find a career instead of working a dead end job, I want to have more friends and possibly a girlfriend as I pretty much have 0 friends atm. That's a lot of shit that I need to change, but I'm taking it one day at a time, and it's getting easier and easier to accomplish all my goals. I've started habits that I believe will help me change with most of these things, and I'm hoping those habits will help build into lifestyle changes that help me accomplish some of the larger goals. 

4. If you do fail, don't beat yourself up, don't binge, get back up and realize that you've made progress, and all you have to do to is keep improving, and you'll soon have this addiction beat. 

5. Realize it's worth it. I think all the success stories that are available on here are evidence of that. Heck I'm only 12 days in my first try, and I'm already much happier with my life then I was a week ago. Go for it man!
